Lee Heung Soo, a peach farmer, has lived through South Korea’s extraordinary economic rise, but the transformation is hard to see from his vantage point in the country’s southwest.
The 74-year-old grew up with the constant roar of fighter jets overhead as they flew in and out of a nearby military airport and air base in the city of Gwangju, which he suspects damaged his hearing. The military presence had kept developers away even as the rest of South Korea industrialized at breakneck speed.
“I thought it would remain an air base forever,” he said as fighter jets took off and landed. “I never imagined anything like this would come here.”

It is designed for component manufacturers, system suppliers, OEM and ODM teams, distributors, investors, and strategic entrants that need a clear view of end-use demand, design-in dynamics, manufacturing exposure, qualification burden, pricing architecture, and competitive positioning.
The analytical framework is designed to work both for a single specialized component class and for a broader electronic components category, where market structure is shaped by product architecture, performance requirements, standards compliance, design-in cycles, component dependencies, lead times, and channel control rather than by one narrow customs heading alone. Historical analysis typically covers 2012 to 2025, with forward-looking scenarios through 2035.
What questions this report answers
This report is designed to answer the questions that matter most to decision-makers evaluating an electronics, electrical, component, interconnect, or power-system market.

The report is particularly useful in markets where buyers are highly specialized, suppliers differ significantly in technical depth and regulatory readiness, and the commercial landscape cannot be understood only through top-line market size figures. In this context, the study is designed not only to estimate the size of the market, but to explain why the market has that size, what drives its growth, which subsegments are the most attractive, and what it takes to compete successfully within it.
Research methodology and analytical framework
The report is based on an independent analytical methodology that combines deep secondary research, structured evidence review, market reconstruction, and multi-level triangulation. The methodology is designed to support products for which there is no single clean official dataset capturing the full market in a directly usable form.
The study typically uses the following evidence hierarchy:

- patents, conference materials, product pages, technical notes, and commercial documentation;
- public pricing references, OEM/service visibility, and channel evidence;

The analytical framework is built around several linked layers.
First, a scope model defines what is included in the market and what is excluded, ensuring that adjacent products, downstream finished goods, unrelated instruments, or broader chemical categories do not distort the market boundary.

Fifth, a pricing and economics layer evaluates price corridors, cost drivers, complexity premiums, outsourcing logic, margin structure, and switching barriers. articles.summary: South Korea exports surge as AI chip demand powers growth ahead of rate decision  CNBC TV18
articles.full_text:
South Korea's exports surged in October, driven by strong AI chip demand and highlighting economic resilience ahead of the central bank's interest-rate decision. Semiconductor shipments led the gains, jumping over 220 percent year on year.
South Korea's exports continued to grow at a rapid pace in the first 20 days of October, driven by strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI), which boosted chip shipments and highlighted the economy's resilience a day before the central bank's interest-rate decision.
Exports adjusted for the number of working days rose 65.9% year on year, the country's customs office said on Wednesday, October 21. This was slower than the 89.8% increase recorded over the same period in September.
Also Read: Asian markets rally as US AI earnings boost sentiment; Kospi surges up to 3.6%
Without the adjustment, exports climbed 105.4% to $61.6 billion, while imports rose 42.8%, leaving the country with a trade surplus of $14.5 billion. Exports had totalled $71.4 billion in the first 20 days of September.
However, the unadjusted year-on-year figures were difficult to compare because the Chuseok holidays fell in September this year, but in October last year. The working-day-adjusted figure therefore provided a more reliable indication of the underlying trend.
Semiconductors led the gains, with chip exports surging 222.5% to $27.5 billion. Shipments of petroleum products rose 68.3%, while car exports increased by almost 41%.
By destination, shipments to China jumped 154.4%, while exports to the United States rose 154.9%. Exports to Malaysia climbed 363.2%, while those to Singapore increased 121.1%.
The figures provided the Bank of Korea (BOK) with an additional economic indicator ahead of Thursday's policy decision. The central bank was widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged as it assessed the impact of its recent rate rises.
The Bank of Korea (BOK) raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3% earlier in August, marking its second consecutive increase. The move came after stronger-than-expected economic growth and persistent inflation prompted policymakers to act early.
Also Read: Japan’s export growth stays solid, AI-chip trade and cars aid rise
Governor Shin Hyun Song said the bank would maintain a tight monetary policy stance until it was confident that inflation would return to its 2% target.
Headline inflation eased to 2.9% in September from 3.1% a month earlier, but remained above the target. Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stood at 2.8%.

articles.title: Japanese and South Korean Stocks Rally in Tandem; Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix Lead Intraday Gains of Over 4% and 6% - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Japanese and South Korean Stocks Rally in Tandem; Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix Lead Intraday Gains of Over 4% and 6%  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
On October 21, stock markets in Japan and South Korea strengthened in tandem, with memory chip stocks serving as the main force driving the indices higher. The Nikkei 225 opened at 64,885.95, up 1.26%, while South Korea's KOSPI opened up 2% at 5,666.34. Gains widened further after the open, with the Nikkei 225 rising as much as 2%, a gain of nearly 1,300 points, while the KOSPI extended its advance to 3.37%.
At the individual stock level, South Korea's two major memory chipmakers stood out. Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) rose more than 4% intraday, while SK Hynix (000660.KS) gained more than 6%. Shares of South Korean data center technology company Elice jumped 16%, after the stock had plunged 32% on its first day of trading in South Korea.
The rebound came after the KOSPI suffered a sharp decline the previous day. On October 20, the index turned lower after two straight sessions of modest gains, closing down 215.27 points, or 3.73%, its lowest close since April 7. It fell as much as 4.76% intraday, losing the 5,500-point mark. On the flows side, foreign investors and domestic institutions sold in tandem that day: foreign investors recorded net sales of ₩636.7 billion (approximately $480.2 million) on South Korea's securities market, while institutional investors sold a net ₩467 billion (approximately $352.2 million), of which financial investment institutions sold a net ₩241.8 billion (approximately $182.4 million) and pension funds sold a net ₩159 billion (approximately $119.9 million). Individual investors and other corporate entities bought a net ₩838.8 billion (approximately $632.7 million) and ₩261.6 billion (approximately $197.3 million), respectively.

|---|---|
| Nikkei 225 open | 64,885.95, up 1.26% | 
| KOSPI open | 5,666.34, up 2% | 
| KOSPI intraday gain | Widened to as much as 3.37% | 
| Samsung Electronics intraday gain | More than 4% | 
| SK Hynix intraday gain | More than 6% | 
| KOSPI October 20 close | 5,552.74, down 3.73% | 
Note: Index and individual stock moves are intraday data for October 21; the KOSPI figure for the prior trading day is the October 20 closing value.
On the macroeconomic front, Japan's September imports rose 18.9% year-on-year, versus an estimate of 20.4%, while exports rose 16.7%, versus an estimate of 21.3%, with both readings below market expectations. South Korea's September producer price index (PPI) rose 7.7% year-on-year.
Overnight, the three major U.S. stock indices closed mixed, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 0.29%, as 11 constituents advanced and 19 declined. Lam Research fell 3.21%, ARM dropped 3.07%, ASML slipped 0.99%, AMD lost 0.62%, Intel declined 0.37% and Broadcom edged down 0.07%. Memory-related stocks were similarly mixed: Western Digital rose 3.44%, Seagate Technology gained 2.17%, SanDisk fell 0.42%, Micron Technology dropped 0.98% and SK Hynix declined 2.16%.
On the recent weakness in South Korean stocks, JPMorgan offered its assessment in a latest report. The bank argued that South Korean equities are quite cheap by both share price levels and trading metrics, but buyers willing to keep adding positions are disappearing. The report cited a marked slowdown in share buybacks by listed companies as an important reason for the recent decline: buybacks had been the main force supporting the market since late August, but Samsung Electronics has completed its buyback program and SK Hynix's is nearing completion.
Valuation data support that assessment. According to the report, even excluding the two memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the KOSPI's forward price-to-earnings ratio is just 8.4 times, a level lower than it has been about 90% of the time by historical standards. Meanwhile, market expectations for the future earnings of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were repeatedly raised in October, with upgrades particularly pronounced in the industrials, financials and health care sectors. That implies the selloff was driven more by capital flight and risk aversion than by a broad deterioration in corporate profitability.
Still, short-term liquidity conditions remain fragile. JPMorgan estimates that quantitative funds such as CTAs, which automatically buy and sell based on price trends, likely shifted from heavily bullish to betting on declines after the latest rout; with short positions already sizable and share prices clearly oversold, conditions for a short-term rebound are forming. But the bank also cautioned that leveraged funds tracking South Korean stocks remain large in scale and outflows have been limited, and such funds often need to sell stocks passively on big down days, so the market could face another wave of selling before that pressure is absorbed. Investors focused on long-term holdings appear to still be waiting for market volatility to subside before re-entering.
From a market linkage perspective, the KOSPI has seen three instances this year of a 15% cumulative decline over five trading sessions, and is down about 40% from its record high set in June. It fell 17.11% in the first half of October, the worst among major global stock indices. As one of the bellwethers of the global artificial intelligence trade, whether South Korean stocks can stabilize is a useful reference for the direction of the U.S. chip sector. At present, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has shown early signs of stabilizing, while South Korean stocks are still falling, a divergence in the two markets' trajectories.
For investors, the core contradiction in South Korean stocks right now is the divergence between valuations and liquidity: earnings expectations are being raised and valuations sit at historic lows, but fading buybacks, foreign outflows and potential selling pressure from leveraged funds form a triple drag. Whether the strong rebound in the two memory giants on the 21st can continue depends on whether selling pressure truly fades and when long-term money returns to the market.

articles.title: North Korea-China trade reaches post-Covid high as new border bridge opens - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: North Korea-China trade reaches post-Covid high as new border bridge opens  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
North Korea and China hold an opening ceremony for the New Yalu River Bridge on Oct. 15 in footage carried by the state-run Korean Central Television on Oct. 16.YONHAP
Trade between North Korea and China reached $2.27 billion in the first nine months of this year, its highest level since the Covid-19 border lockdowns.
The recent opening of the New Yalu River Bridge — connecting the key trading hubs of Sinuiju in North Korea and Dandong in China — has raised expectations of greater cross-border trade and more frequent people-to-people exchanges.
Bilateral trade from January through September rose sharply to $2.27 billion from $1.9 billion during the same period last year, U.S.-based North Korea-focused news site NK News reported Monday, citing data from China's General Administration of Customs.
China's exports to North Korea increased 12.1 percent to $1.79 billion over the same period, while imports from the North surged 50.4 percent to $483.57 million.
Monthly trade also climbed to $299 million in September, up 25.6 percent from $238 million in August. The September figure was the second-highest monthly total this year, behind only April's $326 million.
Experts attribute the rise in bilateral trade to North Korea's increased imports from China and growing exports of light industrial products, including wigs and fake eyelashes, which are not subject to international sanctions.
North Korea imports human hair from China, processes it into wigs and ships the finished products back across the border as part of an active processing trade.
Bilateral trade has risen steadily since Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the North in June. Still, it remains far short of the $4 billion recorded between January and September 2017, when bilateral trade peaked.
Trade plunged after the United Nations Security Council imposed a series of sweeping sanctions on the regime in the second half of 2017 in response to its advancing nuclear and missile programs. It fell further when Pyongyang sealed its borders to prevent the spread of Covid-19.
“Beijing previously took a cautious approach to trade with Pyongyang as it sought to cultivate an image as a responsible major power," Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said.
"But as its strategic rivalry with the United States has intensified, China has placed greater emphasis on cooperation with North Korea. The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects major overland trade hubs, is likely to further boost trade and people-to-people exchanges between North Korea and China for some time."

South Korea plans $520 billion Samsung and SK hynix chip hub in Gwangju
A public-private push aims to build four AI memory fabs on a former air base, with first mass production targeted for June 2030
South Korea wants its next wave of AI chip wealth to land somewhere other than greater Seoul. The chosen spot is a former military air base in the southwest.
On June 29, 2026, the government unveiled a public-private investment of 800 trillion won, or approximately $520 billion, for a new semiconductor hub in the Gwangju and Jeonnam region. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are set to anchor it.
The plan carries a domestic upside and a diplomatic catch. According to Bloomberg, the hub could help spread AI-driven prosperity into the southwest. It could also become another source of friction between Seoul and Washington.
Four fabs on an old runway
The project centers on the site of the former Gwangju Air Base. That land falls within what is now called the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City.
Samsung and SK hynix are each expected to build two memory chip fabrication plants there, for four in total.
The schedule runs in stages:
- 2027: site preparation expected to be finished
- 2028: construction could potentially begin
- June 2030: target for first mass production
The initial build-out is planned at about two-thirds the scale of SK hynix’s Yongin complex. Officials have left room for the cluster to grow beyond that first phase.
Why the southwest, and why now
President Lee Jae-myung made the case for the region by pointing to four inputs. He cited water, renewable energy, land and labor as strategic advantages for chip production.

The Seoul metropolitan area has been running short on several of those. Land and resource limits around the capital have become a capacity problem. The Gwangju hub is partly a pressure-release valve.
The project already has visible corporate backing. On October 9, 2026, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the site and stressed the need to speed up construction.
What this means for chipmakers, the region and Washington
For Samsung and SK hynix, the hub is a bet that AI memory demand stays strong into the next decade. With first production targeted for June 2030, the plants are aimed at demand several years out, not this quarter’s order book.
The scale of the commitment is the headline number to remember. An 800 trillion won public-private package signals that Seoul views AI memory as a national industrial priority, not just a corporate one.
Infrastructure readiness and talent development remain open questions before the cluster can run at full scale.
Watch the 2027 site preparation milestone as the first real test. If that slips, the 2028 construction start and the June 2030 production target come under pressure. The word “potentially” attached to the 2028 date is doing some work.
The Washington dimension is the wild card. Bloomberg flagged the hub as a potential new point of tension in the US-South Korea relationship.

How Taiwan's New AI Chip Export Controls Could Affect China
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan is preparing to impose stricter export controls on advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers destined for China, a move that could significantly change how the island regulates the international trade of high-performance computing equipment.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed in an October 12 interview with Bloomberg that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its list of controlled export items.
Under the proposed framework, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization could become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
The government has not announced when the new restrictions will take effect.
The proposal represents a potentially significant development for Taiwan, which occupies a central position in the global AI hardware supply chain.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) manufactures advanced chips used by leading technology companies, while Taiwanese manufacturers play a major role in assembling AI servers for international customers.
The new restrictions could therefore affect not only chip shipments but also the movement of complete computing systems.
What AI chip export restrictions does Taiwan already have?
Taiwan already operates a strategic high-tech export control system, including controls on sensitive technologies and restrictions involving designated entities.
Companies exporting controlled products must comply with applicable licensing requirements and restrictions on prohibited destinations or end users.
Taiwan has also expanded restrictions involving certain Chinese technology companies, including Huawei and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).
However, these existing controls are not identical to the broader restrictions now being proposed.
The central issue is whether Taiwan can more directly regulate shipments of advanced AI hardware to China, including products that may be diverted through intermediaries.
The proposed measures would strengthen the domestic legal framework for controlling certain shipments.
They should not be interpreted as a blanket ban on every semiconductor or server exported to China.
The exact product categories, technical thresholds, licensing exemptions, and enforcement procedures will depend on the final regulations.
What is Taiwan planning to change?
According to Kung, Taiwan intends to add advanced AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled export list.
The measures are intended to align more closely with restrictions imposed by the United States.
Washington has limited China's access to certain advanced AI accelerators and semiconductor technologies on national security grounds.
Taiwan's proposed changes could make it harder for companies to use Taiwanese manufacturing and export channels to circumvent those restrictions.
Crucially, the government is also seeking stronger domestic enforcement powers.
Under the proposed framework, unauthorized exports of newly controlled AI hardware could be prosecuted directly under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
That would differ from situations in which authorities must rely on other existing legal provisions to investigate suspected smuggling or misrepresentation.
However, criminal liability would depend on the final legal framework, the goods involved, and the specific conduct.
Why does the United States want Taiwan to tighten export controls?
The United States has sought to restrict China's access to advanced computing hardware that could support military applications, intelligence operations, and sophisticated artificial intelligence systems.
But export controls become less effective when restricted products can be purchased through intermediaries or redirected through international supply chains.
Taiwan is especially important because of its role in semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly.
Even when a chip is designed by an American company, its production, packaging, integration, or final system assembly may involve Taiwanese businesses.
That creates a need for coordination across jurisdictions.
In his October interview, Kung linked Taiwan's planned adjustments to commitments made under the 2026 US–Taiwan trade agreement.
Closer coordination could reduce differences between the two countries' regulatory systems, although the precise scope of the Taiwanese measures remains to be announced.
How could the restrictions affect Nvidia and Taiwan's AI server manufacturers?
The potential impact depends on the products covered and the destination of shipments.
Nvidia designs AI accelerators that are manufactured through a global supply chain involving TSMC and other partners.
Taiwanese manufacturers also assemble complete servers incorporating these processors.
A restriction covering only certain semiconductor products would have a different effect from one covering finished AI servers.
For example, a complete server may contain multiple accelerators, memory, networking components, and supporting hardware.
Regulating finished systems could reduce opportunities to circumvent chip-specific restrictions by exporting assembled equipment.
Manufacturers would need to evaluate product classifications, customer identities, ultimate end users, and licensing obligations.
However, it would be premature to estimate the financial impact on individual companies before the government publishes the controlled-item definitions.
Why has AI chip smuggling become a major issue?
Advanced AI accelerators are expensive and strategically important products.
Restrictions on their sale to China have created incentives for unauthorized resale, diversion, and complex procurement arrangements.
Authorities in several jurisdictions have investigated suspected attempts to move restricted computing equipment through intermediaries.
For Taiwan, the challenge is particularly sensitive because of the concentration of semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly on the island.
The issue also raises questions about the responsibilities of manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, and overseas customers.
Existing CommonWealth reporting on the Supermicro AI hardware controversy examined how international trade restrictions can intersect with Taiwan's technology supply chains.
The proposed export-control changes would give Taiwanese authorities an additional policy instrument to address such risks.
Could Taiwan's new rules stop China from obtaining advanced AI chips?
Stricter controls could make unauthorized shipments more difficult and increase the legal risks for participants.
However, export restrictions alone cannot guarantee that prohibited hardware will never reach China.
Their effectiveness depends on enforcement, international cooperation, product traceability, and the ability to identify indirect shipments.
The final impact will also depend on whether the new regulations cover individual chips, assembled servers, or both.
For Taiwan, the challenge is to strengthen compliance without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate technology trade.
FAQs
Has Taiwan banned AI chip exports to China?
No blanket ban has been established by the announced proposal. Taiwan already has controls on certain sensitive products and entities, and the government plans to expand restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
When will Taiwan's new AI chip export controls take effect?
As of October 19, 2026, the government has not announced an implementation date.
Which AI chips will be restricted?
The government has indicated that advanced semiconductors and AI servers will be included. Detailed technical specifications and product classifications have not yet been announced.
Will exporting AI chips to China become a criminal offense?
Unauthorized exports of products covered by the proposed new controls could become subject to criminal prosecution under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act once the measures take effect. This does not mean every chip export to China would be illegal.
Will the restrictions affect TSMC?
They could affect compliance requirements for relevant products and transactions involving Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain. The direct implications will depend on the final rules and existing contractual and regulatory arrangements.
Are Taiwan's export controls the same as those of the United States?
No. Taiwan and the United States operate separate legal systems. Taiwan is seeking closer alignment, but companies must evaluate their obligations under each applicable jurisdiction.
The Bottom Line
Taiwan's planned AI export controls are significant because they could close a gap between the island's central role in manufacturing advanced computing hardware and its ability to enforce restrictions on unauthorized shipments.
But the measures remain a proposal until the government publishes and implements the relevant regulations.
For companies operating across Taiwan, China, and the United States, the most important questions are which products will be covered, what licenses will be required, and how the new rules will be enforced.
Policy status: October 19, 2026. The proposed expansion of export controls has been publicly confirmed, but the implementation date and complete product coverage have not been announced.

articles.title: Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
North Korea’s balancing act is back in the spotlight. In September, it opened its first road bridge with Russia. Just last week, North Korea opened a similar one with China. Pyongyang’s land bridge with Russia will strengthen the bilateral arms trade while the one with China will provide it with energy products, raw materials, and heavy equipment for domestic consumption.
The two bridges are a microcosm of how North Korea seeks to benefit from improved relations with Moscow and Beijing. North Korea is looking for military assistance from Russia and economic help from China. The clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
North Korea has decades of experience when it comes to managing relations with Moscow and Beijing for its own benefits. In July 1961, the country signed two separate alliance treaties with the Soviet Union and China by exploiting the Sino-Soviet Split. The more bitter Moscow and Beijing were toward each other, the more willing they were to meet Pyongyang’s demands.
The combined Soviet and Chinese economic aid meant North Korea enjoyed a relatively higher living standard compared to its communist peers China and North Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s. Its military was also on par with that of South Korea thanks to generous Soviet and Chinese transfers of weapons and technologies.
However, North Korea’s balancing act failed when the Soviet Union encountered economic trouble and began to amend ties with China in 1986. Moscow was no longer interested in competing with China for influence over North Korea and began to cut back economic and military aid. China in turn reduced the amount of military and economic support due to Soviet retrenchment.
Without a split to leverage, Pyongyang could not demand that Moscow and Beijing maintain a generous level of aid. North Korea went bankrupt in the 1990s, and its military slipped behind South Korea’s.
North Korea has now crafted a new playbook on how to get Russia and China to support Pyongyang’s goals – even in the absence of a split. In the past, North Korea handled Moscow and Beijing by having them compete over both military and economic aid. Now, North Korea balances between its two patrons by assigning them a separate domain of cooperation suitable to their specific needs.
North Korea’s outreach to Russia revolves around military exchanges to get Moscow to assist in the development of its weapons of mass destruction program. North Korea leverages Russia’s need for weapons, troops, and ammunition for the war against Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s military technology. In return, Russia has been vocal about its support for North Korea’s nuclear program and even pledged to defend Pyongyang under the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
North Korea-Russia arms trade nearly doubled from 2023 to 2025, growing from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion. This amount overshadows the food and fuel trade, which reached a record high of $34 million in 2024. North Korean laborers in Russia work in drone factories or in warzones along the Russia-Ukraine border. Pyongyang is also stressing its blood sacrifice for Russia’s war to remind Moscow of its military debt.
North Korea’s outreach to China takes on a completely different tone. Pyongyang emphasizes economic cooperation with China because it understands Beijing desires political and economic stability on the Korean Peninsula. In 2026, bilateral trade increased to $1.5 billion, up 19.6 percent compared to the first half of 2025. This marks a record high since China imposed sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear test in 2017. Noticeably, weapons made up little of the trade rebound. Unlike their peers in Russia, North Korean laborers in China mostly work in the food service and textile industry.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June, he and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un agreed to bolster ties in politics, economy, and culture. The military aspect of the Kim-Xi summit was largely absent from public view although the visit corresponded with the 65th anniversary of the signing of the 1961 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Unlike Russia and North Korea, China and North Korea didn’t publicly praise the mutual defense clause in the treaty. However, Pyongyang got Beijing to quietly drop “denuclearization” in its North Korea policy and to stop enforcing international sanctions.
Russia and China have been comfortable with North Korea’s division of labor. Neither Moscow nor Beijing sees each other’s expanding cooperation with North Korea as a threat. China accepts Pyongyang sending troops to Russia’s war in Ukraine so long as North Korea’s participation doesn’t undermine China’s desire for stability in Northeast Asia. China even harbored a Russian ship involved in the North Korea-Russia arms trade, which had to be conducted by air and sea routes before the new land bridge was opened.
For its part, although Russia’s 2024 alliance treaty with North Korea mirrors the 1961 treaty, Moscow doesn’t treat it as a rival to China’s 1961 alliance treaty. Russia even supports trilateral dialogue with China and North Korea over Chinese vessels’ use of the Tumen River for access to the Sea of Japan. Russia’s support for North Korea’s nuclear and conventional forces modernization doesn’t come at China’s expense as North Korea doesn’t plan on invading South Korea anytime soon.
From North Korea’s perspective, selling weapons to Russia and wigs to China means its alliances with both are complimentary instead of competitive. Pyongyang can secure long-term support from Russia and China not through their spite toward each other but through their genuine interest in fostering a stable ally in the Asia-Pacific.
Thanks to Russian and Chinese backing, North Korea’s economy is booming and its military is undergoing the most comprehensive modernization program since 1991. Russia’s and China’s support also gives North Korea stronger diplomatic leverage in case it decides to restart dialogue with the United States. Importantly, North Korea doesn’t base its foreign policy on the state of Beijing-Moscow relations like it did during the Cold War. If either Russia or China loses interest in bolstering North Korea’s economy and military at some point in the future, the other patron will not reduce aid just because it has “won” the competition.

articles.title: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed?
Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.
What Pyongyang Learned From Hanoi
The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement.
Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.
North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.
North Korea did not begin identifying itself as a nuclear weapon state in 2022. It had already codified that status in a 2013 law “consolidating the position of nuclear weapons state for self-defense.” Article 9 of that law, however, expressed support for international nuclear disarmament efforts. The omission of that provision from the 2022 law was therefore significant.
The 2022 law not only entrenched nuclear possession as a permanent foundation of national strategy but also called for qualitative and quantitative improvements in nuclear forces in response to external threats and changes in the international nuclear balance. In this context, a freeze on nuclear weapons production or a reduction in its nuclear arsenal could conflict with this policy if North Korea’s security environment remained unchanged.
Setting the Terms for Renewed Talks
North Korea’s recent statements on relations with Washington indicate that it expects changes in U.S. policy before talks resume, while treating its nuclear possession as non-negotiable.
In October 2025, Trump publicly expressed his desire to meet Kim Jong Un again during his trip to Asia. That didn’t eventuate, but Trump is reportedly looking at the possibility of a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia in November 2026.
At the Ninth Workers’ Party Congress in February 2026, Kim Jong Un stated that relations with the United States could improve if Washington respected North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state and abandoned its hostile policy. He thus linked improved relations to a change in Washington’s attitude toward a nuclear-armed North Korea and its policy toward Pyongyang.
In August, Trump again expressed interest in meeting Kim and ordered a reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and an authoritative voice for the regime, dismissed the move as insufficient. She argued that holding the exercises at all demonstrated Washington’s hostility. Kim Yo Jong’s response suggested that Pyongyang wanted the exercises halted altogether, rather than merely scaled back, before agreeing to talks. In the same statement, she also criticized South Korea’s push to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.
In September, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea’s nuclear status was irreversible. She rejected the coexistence of confrontation and dialogue in relations with North Korea and argued that a geopolitical realignment centered on a nuclear-armed North Korea was inevitable. Her statement reinforced the message that Washington could not maintain policies Pyongyang regarded as hostile and expect dialogue to follow.
North Korea has long sought security guarantees and an end to Washington’s hostile policy. The difference now is that Pyongyang treats its nuclear possession as non-negotiable and expects changes in U.S. attitudes and military policy before talks resume. A reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises alone appears insufficient to meet its demands. Its criticism of South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine plans also suggests concern about potential U.S. support for such capabilities.
This departs from the Singapore agreement, which paired a commitment to denuclearization with improved relations and the establishment of a peace regime. Pyongyang now seeks U.S. policy changes as the starting point for diplomacy, rather than as part of a bargain over giving up its nuclear weapons.
North Korea’s strategy notwithstanding, its ability to change U.S. policy is not guaranteed. Despite Trump’s efforts to engage Pyongyang, the United States, South Korea, and Japan continue to reaffirm the goal of North Korea’s denuclearization, while Washington maintains its defense commitments to its allies.
Pyongyang may see no need to rush into talks. It continues to build up its nuclear forces, citing security threats, while strengthening ties with its partners.
In September 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported signs of a new uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of expanded operations at Kangson. North Korea has also recently increased the frequency of its missile tests. Meanwhile, expanding military cooperation with Russia and improving relations with China are giving Pyongyang greater room to resist international pressure, including sanctions. Both countries oppose further sanctions on North Korea and have become quieter on its denuclearization.
North Korea may believe that time is on its side: As its nuclear capabilities grow and its diplomatic options expand, Washington may eventually have no choice but to enter talks on the basis that North Korea will retain its nuclear weapons.
How the United States Should Respond
Washington’s first task is to clarify the conditions under which North Korea is willing to negotiate and the agenda it is prepared to discuss. Some experts argue that a nuclear freeze or reductions should serve as interim goals if complete denuclearization cannot be achieved in the short term. This may be a realistic alternative for the United States, but Washington should not assume that Pyongyang will accept it as a topic for negotiation. North Korea may instead demand that negotiations focus on regional security issues or insist on changes in U.S. policy before agreeing to talks.
To clarify these issues, working-level meetings should precede any new North Korea-U.S. summit. Washington must coordinate closely with Seoul and Tokyo before negotiating measures that affect their security. If Pyongyang raises concerns about U.S. military activities on the Korean Peninsula, Washington should assess whether its demands can be addressed through reciprocal military measures.
Discussing regional security does not necessarily mean recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state or weakening allied military readiness. With South Korea’s agreement, for example, the United States could consider adjusting the scale or format of joint exercises in exchange for limits on North Korean exercises in specific areas, with arrangements for both sides to verify compliance. Once military crisis-management measures are in place and the security environment improves, Washington could argue that Pyongyang should move toward a nuclear freeze or reductions.
The United States must also challenge North Korea’s calculation that time is on its side. Maintaining existing sanctions and deterrence alone is unlikely to change Pyongyang’s strategic judgment. The United States should make clear that North Korea’s continued nuclear buildup could lead South Korea and Japan to strengthen their military capabilities and fuel calls in both countries for nuclear weapons of their own. An offer to discuss regional security should accompany that message. The aim should be to create incentives for diplomacy without triggering another arms race.
Washington should use security talks to pursue reciprocal military measures and build a path toward limits on North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. Knowing what each side is willing to offer before the next summit would improve the chances of reaching an agreement.

articles.title: Crash! KOSPI in free fall? South Korea stock market down another 5%, tanks 40% from record high- What’s driving AI rout? - Livemint

articles.full_text:
South Korea’s stock market is facing a deepening sell-off as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending, semiconductor valuations and rising financing costs rattle investors. The benchmark KOSPI fell another 5% on Tuesday, extending its losses as investors pulled back from AI-linked stocks.
The index had surged earlier this year, with its gains reaching around 116% at its record close in June. However, the subsequent correction has erased much of that rally, leaving the KOSPI up approximately 30% in 2026. The index has also fallen 39% from its peak of 9,386 earlier this year to 5,493.24 currently.
The sell-off accelerated in July, when the KOSPI fell 22%, and continued into October, with the index losing another 17% through October 16. The latest pressure has been particularly severe for semiconductor stocks, which account for a significant share of South Korea’s market.
SK Hynix shares have plunged around 35% from their peak, while Samsung Electronics has fallen approximately 22%. The weakness has spread to newer AI-linked businesses, too, with data-centre infrastructure company Elice Inc. dropping as much as 32% during its trading debut in Seoul.
The latest decline follows a global sell-off in AI and semiconductor stocks that wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value from 20 of the world’s most valuable AI and semiconductor companies last week.
South Korea has been particularly vulnerable because of its heavy dependence on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Together, the two companies accounted for 44% of the KOSPI in May. As a result, a sharp decline in either stock can have a significant impact on the broader index.
Stronger-than-expected US inflation data has added to the uncertainty. Hotter inflation can reduce the likelihood of interest-rate cuts and revive expectations of rate hikes, raising borrowing costs and putting pressure on highly valued growth stocks.
According to a Reuters report, OpenAI told investors last week that its annualised revenue for September was nearly $50 billion, below a figure it had indicated earlier. At a separate event, the company had previously said its September revenue run rate was approaching $70 billion. The discrepancy reportedly stemmed largely from an effort to compare its revenue directly with that of rival Anthropic.
Concerns about funding are also emerging from within the semiconductor industry. Earlier this week, Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan said capital could become a bigger constraint on AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity.
Daniel Munday, Principal Analyst at VT Markets, said the combination of inflation concerns and doubts about AI financing had intensified the sell-off across Asian markets.
“Hotter US CPI revived Fed hike bets, then cautious Fed comments pulled them back. At the same time, AI financing worries hit US tech, with CoreWeave and Oracle sold off on debt fears. Asia took the hit, and the KOSPI closed down 7.57%, its seventh straight loss, with foreign investors heavy sellers,” Munday said.
Munday also noted that US Treasury yields and the dollar eased overnight as investors sought safer assets. A Bloomberg report suggesting China held more US debt than official data showed also influenced market sentiment.
The sell-off has intensified the debate over whether AI stocks can sustain their earnings growth and justify their valuations. Some analysts believe investors may need to diversify beyond the sector rather than remain heavily exposed to the AI trade.
In his latest GREED & fear note, Jefferies Global Head of Equity Strategy Chris Wood highlighted a warning from the brokerage’s global quantitative strategy team that “it has become time to diversify beyond AI.”
The report projects earnings growth for global AI stocks to slow from nearly 100% in 2026 to 30% in 2027 and 22% in 2028. By comparison, earnings growth for global stocks excluding AI is expected to decline from 16% in 2026 to 9% in both 2027 and 2028.
Wood has also highlighted rising borrowing costs as a central factor in the AI spending boom, raising questions about how long companies and investors can sustain the current pace of investment.
Munday said a rebound was possible after such a rapid fall, especially as US yields and the dollar eased. However, he cautioned that markets with heavy semiconductor exposure, including South Korea, Taiwan and Japan, could remain volatile until concerns about AI spending and interest rates subside.
Investors will be watching the US Federal Reserve’s October 28 meeting, further inflation data, oil prices and tensions in the Middle East.

REUTERS
October 20, 2026 at 16:01 JST
A screen displays the company logo for semiconductor and chipmaker GlobalFoundries Inc. during the company's IPO at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square in New York City on Oct. 28, 2021. (Reuters/ File Photo)
Japan is in the midst of a major push to revive its chip sector, but its latest investments show how Tokyo is being pulled into helping the U.S. build up its own semiconductor industry.
Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state, under a deal announced last week by GlobalFoundries, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co.
It is part of a pledge to invest $550 billion in the U.S. made with the Trump administration in return for lower tariffs. Under that deal, the US president - not Japan - gets to select the projects.
That shows the price Japan is paying to maintain trade relations with the U.S., the world’s largest economy and its closest security partner. But the pledge, agreed to in July 2025, will not do much to resurrect Japan’s chip industry and will have a limited impact on improving its supply chain resilience, experts said.
“Japan is funding US semiconductor capacity without necessarily gaining much of the advanced chip technology or domestic manufacturing capabilities it wants,” said Nori Chiou, investment director at White Oak Capital.
U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on countries around the world last year to try to shrink the U.S. trade deficit, with governments in South Korea and Taiwan also making investment pledges.
It is not the first time that Japan has been pushed around by the U.S. over chips. In the 1980s, Japan - the globally dominant chipmaking centre - agreed to restrict semiconductor exports to the U.S., with memories of that period remaining a sore point for bureaucrats in Tokyo.
“Investment in the U.S. is, ultimately, a measure for dealing with Trump. It is essentially about buying time in order to maintain the U.S.-Japan relationship,” said a Japanese government source, who declined to be named as the issue is politically contentious.
INDISPENSABLE PARTNER
Earlier this month, Japanese industry minister Ryosei Akazawa, when asked if corporate investment in the U.S. could weaken investment in Japan, said: “We believe that investment in the U.S. and domestic growth investment are entirely compatible.”
“Japan is a partner the U.S. cannot do without to maintain its supremacy as a hegemonic power in economic, security and technological terms,” Akazawa said last week. He negotiated the investment pledge in a previous role.
The investment will benefit Japanese equipment manufacturers like Tokyo Electron, whose earnings have swelled due to the AI boom, while customers will include Renesas Electronics , GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen has said.
Tokyo needs to arrange financing for the chip factories, with other previously announced projects including oil and natural gas-related investments and small nuclear reactors.
The state-backed Japan Bank for International Cooperation and commercial banks will provide loans, with guarantees from Nippon Export and Investment Insurance.
Japanese banks have been reluctant to participate due to the cost of acquiring the large amount of U.S. dollars required, with Tokyo looking to JPMorgan and other US banks for help, Reuters has reported.
Japan is hardly flush with cash, with the highest debt-to-GDP ratio in the developed world and investor concerns about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s fiscal expansion plans.
REGARD INVESTMENT AS A TAX
Takaichi has ambitions to pour public-private investment totaling some $2.3 trillion through fiscal 2040 across 17 strategic Japanese sectors, including AI and chips.
As economic security has become front of mind, the government’s thinking has shifted to the view that having a manufacturing base in Japan is extremely important, said a government source who declined to be named because the matter is politically contentious.
Japan’s flagship chip-sector project is Rapidus, which seeks to mass-produce cutting-edge chips starting next year but is widely viewed with scepticism by the industry.
Tokyo is also backing robot AI company Noetra and has provided subsidies to TSMC, Micron and Kioxia to locate chipmaking capacity in Japan.
If U.S.-made chips can be integrated into Japan’s semiconductor supply chain, there is no need for everything to be produced domestically, the first government source said.
“Whether (the chip factory investment) works out or not, Japan will just have to regard it as a tax,” said Atsushi Osanai, a professor at Waseda University.

Korea’s $1 Trillion Tech Bet Gwangju Chip Hub Could Reshape the Semiconductor Industry
South Korea is planning a massive semiconductor manufacturing hub in Gwangju, bringing Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix into a project that could reshape the country’s technology industry. However, the ambitious plan faces a major challenge: expanding domestic chip production without provoking fresh trade tensions with US President Donald Trump.
The proposed development forms part of a broader 1,350 trillion won ($1 trillion) investment push covering semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres. At its centre is an 800 trillion won investment plan for four semiconductor fabrication plants, or fabs, at a site currently occupied by a military airport.
For investors, the project raises important questions about future chip manufacturing capacity, AI-related demand, infrastructure costs and the possibility of new US trade restrictions.

Korea’s $1 Trillion Tech Bet : Samsung and SK Hynix Face a Major Investment Opportunity
President Lee Jae Myung wants to transform the southwestern Honam region into a major semiconductor hub. The plan could bring industrial investment and employment to an area that has historically lagged behind South Korea’s main industrial centres.
The first of the four fabs is expected to begin mass production by 2030. The wider Gwangju cluster is projected to require around 23,000 workers, potentially attracting employees and businesses from other regions.
However, the scale of the proposed investment should not be confused with confirmed spending already under way. Construction timelines, the pace of investment and the eventual expansion of production remain uncertain.
Economist Jeong-Woo Park of Nomura Holdings said the broader investment programme could raise South Korea’s medium-term growth potential, although uncertainty over execution makes it difficult to incorporate the full impact into forecasts.
What is South Korea planning?
- A new semiconductor hub: President Lee Jae Myung’s government plans to establish a major semiconductor manufacturing cluster in Gwangju and the wider Honam region in southwestern South Korea.
- 800 trillion won for four chip factories: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are expected to invest approximately 800 trillion won in four semiconductor fabrication plants, commonly called fabs. The investment was reported at around $592 billion in September 2026, although the dollar equivalent varies with exchange rates.
- A broader 1,350 trillion won investment push: The semiconductor project forms part of a wider government-backed investment strategy covering semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence (AI) and AI data centres.
- A second major production base: The objective is to establish a second major semiconductor manufacturing centre outside the Seoul metropolitan region, expanding South Korea’s capacity to meet growing demand for chips used in AI systems.
Trump’s Tariff Threat Adds Uncertainty to South Korea’s Chip Strategy
Washington wants South Korean companies to expand manufacturing in the United States rather than concentrate more investment at home.
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Bloomberg Television that South Korean companies need to build in the US and warned of possible fresh tariffs if Seoul does not comply.
The comments create a difficult balancing act for the South Korean government. It wants to develop domestic manufacturing while maintaining strong economic and security ties with Washington.
The US State Department said South Korea has been among the leading investors in the United States, adding that Korean investments support efforts to revitalise American manufacturing.
The relocation of Gwangju’s military airport also requires careful coordination. The site has a role in contingency military planning and includes facilities reserved for US military use. Seoul has not confirmed whether Washington has approved the proposed relocation.

Why has Gwangju been selected?
- Location: Gwangju is approximately 266 kilometres from Seoul and has a population of around 1.4 million people.
- Government-owned land: The proposed site is the existing military airport, covering approximately 8.2 square kilometres. Government ownership could reduce the difficulty of acquiring thousands of privately owned plots.
- Transport connectivity: The location offers access to high-speed rail, roads and regional transport infrastructure, helping companies move workers, equipment and materials.
- Regional development: The Honam region has historically attracted less large-scale industrial investment than South Korea’s capital region and southeastern industrial belt.
- Economic revival: The proposed chip cluster could create new industrial activity, attract supporting businesses and provide employment opportunities in an area that has experienced economic stagnation and the departure of younger workers.
The government selected the Gwangju airport site in July 2026, according to The Korea Times.
What role will Samsung and SK Hynix play?
- Samsung Electronics: The South Korean technology giant is expected to participate in developing the new semiconductor manufacturing capacity.
- SK Hynix: The company, a major supplier of memory chips used in AI infrastructure and computing systems, is also expected to establish manufacturing facilities.
- Four semiconductor fabs: The plan envisages four chip plants to expand the country’s manufacturing capacity and support demand associated with AI development.
- AI-driven demand: Advanced computing systems require substantial quantities of memory and other semiconductors. The proposed cluster is intended to help South Korea maintain its position in the global semiconductor industry.
Water and Power Infrastructure Could Delay the Gwangju Project
The proposed semiconductor complex will require substantial resources. The fabs are expected to need approximately 650,000 tonnes of water every day, raising concerns in a region that has experienced severe drought.
The government plans to draw water from nearby reservoirs and recycle treated wastewater. However, environmental experts have questioned whether sufficient backup arrangements would be available during emergencies.
Electricity is another important consideration. South Jeolla province generates roughly twice as much electricity as it consumes, but delivering that power to the proposed chip hub will require additional transmission infrastructure.
New power lines could face resistance from rural communities concerned about environmental damage and the impact of high-voltage towers near their homes.
Why is the project creating tensions with the United States?
- Washington wants more chip production in America: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has argued that South Korean chipmakers should expand manufacturing in the United States and warned that companies failing to do so could face additional tariffs.
- Potential tariff exposure: The Trump administration is considering semiconductor tariff policies linked to domestic manufacturing investment. Such measures could affect the cost competitiveness of Samsung and SK Hynix if they cannot secure favourable treatment.
- A difficult investment decision: Both companies must weigh the benefits of expanding manufacturing in South Korea against the commercial and trade advantages of investing in the US.
- National-security considerations: The Gwangju airport is associated with military operations and is designated to receive US air assets during contingencies. Relocating the facilities therefore requires coordination with Washington.
- A balancing act for Seoul: South Korea wants to strengthen domestic manufacturing and regional development while maintaining its security partnership and economic relationship with the United States.
Why must the military airport be relocated?
- The land is central to the project: The existing airport site is intended to accommodate the proposed semiconductor complex.
- Relocation plans have faced delays: Governments have discussed moving the military facilities for years, but the process has remained unresolved.
- The original timeline: The government had planned to relocate or temporarily disperse military facilities by mid-2028.
- The president wants to accelerate the process: Lee Jae Myung has directed officials to examine ways to move faster.
- US coordination is essential: Some parts of the site are reserved for US military use in an emergency, making the relocation more complicated than a normal land-development project.
- Construction depends on execution: Government ownership simplifies land acquisition, but it does not eliminate the need to resolve military, security and infrastructure issues.

What Samsung and SK Hynix Investors Should Watch Next
Beyond construction, Gwangju must attract thousands of workers and provide suitable housing, education, healthcare and other services. Local residents have welcomed the proposal, but some remain sceptical after decades of delayed airport relocation plans.
For investors, the key developments to watch are confirmation of funding, approval for military relocation, progress on water and electricity infrastructure, and the response from Washington.
The Gwangju semiconductor hub could support South Korea’s long-term economic growth and expand domestic chip production. Yet its eventual impact on Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and investor portfolios will depend on whether the government can turn its ambitious investment plan into operating factories without significant delays or additional trade barriers.

articles.title: Japan ‘months’ from running out of critical rare earth as China squeezes supply - Financial Times
articles.summary: Japan ‘months’ from running out of critical rare earth as China squeezes supply  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Japan is months from running out of supplies of yttrium, a critical metal, and has asked the US to push China to ease rare earth export controls that threaten severe disruption to the global automotive, defence and chip industries.
Tokyo made the entreaty to the US government and American blue-chip companies, according to people familiar with the matter in Washington and Tokyo.
Washington has urged China in recent months to increase the flow of rare earths, including yttrium — a heat-resistant metal crucial to manufacturing vehicles, jet engines and semiconductors — to the US and its allies. US defence supply chains rely on components made in Japan that contain yttrium.
Unless Beijing changes tack or western allies find substitutes or additional stockpiles, shortages could emerge as early as the end of this year, Japanese government officials and trading house executives said.
“We’re in a serious situation to keep supplying downstream industries,” said a Japanese government official. “Stockpiles are decreasing and rare earth saving efforts have a limit.”
“The timeline is not years, it’s months and how to survive next year,” the official added. “If everyone acts right now, then it will be OK. If everyone ignores the problem, then it will be a systemic risk to the world economy.”
China dominates the supply chain for mining and processing rare earths, leverage it has used in response to US President Donald Trump’s trade war.
China has also strengthened export controls against Japan in response to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comments last year about the existential threat to Japan from a conflict over Taiwan, which outraged Beijing.
Yttrium shortages have become the biggest pain point for Japanese materials groups. The metal is used to coat engines and plasma-etching chambers for chip manufacturing.
Yttrium oxide prices outside China have skyrocketed to $1,150 per kilogramme, a 179-fold increase versus two years ago, compared with $9 per kilogramme in China, according to price assessments by Argus.
US and Japanese officials have held numerous talks about the yttrium crunch, including last month in Washington when US energy department officials and Japanese industry ministry officials convened a critical minerals “rapid response group”.
At the meeting, which came two weeks before Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House, the Japanese government clarified the gravity of the situation in the hope that US businesses affected by the shortages would also lobby Washington to raise concerns with Beijing.
The US has complained that China is not fulfilling its pledge to ease rare earth controls under the trade truce the two sides reached last October. After Trump met Xi in Beijing in May, China reiterated that pledge to “address US concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths . . . including yttrium”.
A senior US official told the FT last month that China was fulfilling two-thirds of its rare earth commitments to the US, and was only allowing Japan to procure the bare minimum of its needs.
US officials have told Beijing that the US will not export jet engines needed for the Comac C919 — China’s first domestically made airliner — as production has been constrained by the lack of yttrium, which is critical to making turbines.
China also agreed to buy 200 Boeing jets when Trump visited Beijing in May. But the deal has not been completed, partly due to complications related to critical minerals.
Erin Browne, the top US Treasury official for international affairs, told the FT that rare earths were essential to the production of Boeing aircraft and jet engines.
“In order to produce aircraft, you need rare earths,” said Browne. “They’re all sort of under the same umbrella, which is that in order to . . . export engines, you also need rare earths.”
Japan’s economy ministry and the US Treasury, which is leading the trade talks with China, declined to comment specifically on yttrium.
A senior Treasury official said reliable access to critical minerals was “essential to US economic and national security”.
“Export restrictions that disrupt the flow of critical minerals are a serious concern,” the US official said.
The Chinese embassy in the US did not respond to a request for comment.
“It is rightful panic in Japan,” said Gracelin Baskaran, head of the critical minerals security programme at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “They are probably going to have to suffer for the time being.”

articles.title: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers - Tech Times
articles.summary: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry formally approved a revised production plan for TSMC's second fabrication plant in Kumamoto Prefecture on October 16, 2026, certifying what will become Japan's first facility capable of manufacturing 3-nanometer logic semiconductors. The approval is a genuine milestone — but the story behind the numbers is more technically revealing than the headline suggests. The original plan called for 48,000 wafers per month at 6nm and 12nm. The approved plan calls for 6,000 wafers per month at 3nm. That 87.5% capacity reduction is not a setback. It is a direct consequence of what 3nm manufacturing actually requires — and of who makes the equipment that enables it.
Japan's Node Upgrade — and the Volume Reckoning It Reveals
When TSMC first laid out plans for the Kumamoto second fab in February 2024, the blueprint called for producing 6nm and 12nm chips at a monthly capacity of 48,000 wafers, according to the JASM second fab announced in 2024 — a volume-first approach geared largely toward Japan's automotive and industrial sectors. Under the now-approved plan, the facility will produce 3nm chips at an initial monthly target of just 6,000 wafers, an 87.5% reduction in output volume compared to the prior design. METI approved the plan change on October 16.
The reduction is not a sign of diminished ambition. It reflects what happens when a facility moves from mature-node mass production into frontier-node manufacturing. At 3nm, a chip requires extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography — a technology that prints circuits with light at a wavelength of just 13.5 nanometers (0.000000053 inches), roughly one-fifteenth of a wavelength of visible light. EUV lithography is used on more than 20 critical layers at the 3nm node, compared to approximately 14 layers at 5nm. And only one company in the world is the sole manufacturer of EUV systems at commercial scale: ASML, the Dutch equipment maker.
TSMC and METI framed the revised plan explicitly around the requirements of 3nm manufacturing, which demands EUV equipment and carries a significantly heavier investment burden per wafer than the more mature nodes it replaces. METI's Director of the Information Industry Division, Tomonari Nanbu told reporters that "given the progress of AI transformation, 3nm cutting-edge logic semiconductors that power AI are indispensable," signaling that the ministry views the node upgrade as a strategic necessity.
TSMC has indicated that the 6,000-wafer figure represents only the first phase, and that production capacity will expand depending on the level of additional government support it receives.
Why EUV Scarcity — Not Strategy — Governs the Capacity Figure
Understanding why the Kumamoto II fab will start at 6,000 wafers per month instead of 48,000 requires understanding EUV tool availability.
ASML's EUV systems — the NXE series, which uses an optical system with a numerical aperture of 0.33 — are the workhorses of every advanced-node fab in the world. Each machine uses EUV plasma generation technology in which a pulsed laser fires at liquid tin droplets more than 50,000 times per second, producing photons at the 13.5nm wavelength that then pass through a reflective optical system to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.
ASML produces roughly 50 to 60 EUV systems per year globally. Every major foundry — TSMC in Taiwan and Arizona, Samsung in South Korea, Intel in the United States, and now Rapidus in Hokkaido — competes for allocation from that limited production line. Each EUV tool costs in excess of $150 million; installing and qualifying a single tool at a new fab takes months. A 3nm production line requires multiple such tools running in concert.
The 6,000-wafer-per-month figure represents what EUV tool allocation and yield ramp-up can realistically support at a new Japanese site in the 2026–2028 installation window, given that TSMC is simultaneously prioritizing equipment for its Fab 21 Phase 2 in Arizona (targeting 3nm production in the second half of 2027) and its continued 3nm and 2nm expansion in Taiwan. There was earlier reporting of a 15,000-wafer monthly figure when Taiwan approved the 3nm investment in March 2026; the official METI-certified plan lists 6,000 wafers per month. METI's official documents do not explain the difference, but the discrepancy is consistent with a first-phase ceiling set by tool availability rather than demand.
METI is explicitly considering increasing its support, and METI included the subsidy request in its fiscal year 2027 preliminary budget — a process that will determine whether TSMC can raise the 6,000-wafer ceiling before mass production begins in December 2028.
Subsidy Structure and Investment Scale
METI designated the Kumamoto II plant as a subsidy recipient under Japan's semiconductor reindustrialization program. The government originally planned to provide ¥732 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in subsidies tied to the prior 6nm/12nm plan. With the revised blueprint now approved, that figure has been adjusted to ¥645.15 billion (approximately $4.1 billion), reflecting the reduced initial production volume, as documented in the METI official revised plan document.
The first Kumamoto fab's subsidy was also revised downward — from ¥476 billion to ¥409.5 billion (approximately $2.6 billion). Between the two plants, total committed public support fell from ¥1.208 trillion to ¥1.055 trillion (approximately $6.7 billion). However, METI is considering increasing the second fab's support as the full scale of the 3nm investment becomes clearer. TSMC's own statement confirmed total Kumamoto capital spending exceeds $23 billion (approximately ¥3.63 trillion) across both facilities.
Timeline: December 2028
Commercial production at the second Kumamoto fab is targeted for December 2028. Under METI's certification conditions, JASM commits to ten-year operation and to increasing production in the event of a domestic shortage — conditions attached to all Japanese government semiconductor subsidies.
The 2028 production date means Kumamoto's 3nm node will come online approximately one year after TSMC's 3nm capacity at its second Arizona fab, where Arizona 3nm production targets 2027 in the second half. That sequence reflects TSMC's global capital allocation priorities — Taiwan first, then Arizona under US CHIPS Act pressure, then Japan — rather than any deficiency in the Japanese site itself.
Kumamoto I Also Revised
METI's October 16 approval package extended to the existing Kumamoto I plant as well. Originally planned to run both 12–16nm and 22–28nm processes at a combined 55,000 wafers per month, the first fab plan revised to 22-28nm phases out all 12–16nm production, concentrating the facility on 22–28nm nodes (plus 40nm processes reserved for Japanese domestic customers) at 45,000 wafers per month across the subsidized facility footprint, and 50,000 wafers per month across the full plant.
JASM attributes this revision to how automotive and industrial customer demand has evolved — an implicit acknowledgment that sluggish electric vehicle adoption has moderated demand for the advanced-mature nodes originally planned for Kumamoto I. The move effectively repositions Kumamoto I as a stable-node workhorse for Sony image sensors, automotive chips, and industrial electronics, freeing the second facility to serve as the campus's leading-edge AI-oriented anchor.
The first fab has been operating since late 2024, when volume production began at 12–28nm. Its resilience was tested on July 28, 2026, when a magnitude 7.1 earthquake halted JASM Fab 1 operations for equipment inspections. The facility recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 5 at the fab site; analysts estimated a one-week shutdown could represent approximately $14 million in potential lost revenue, according to the TSMC Kumamoto earthquake impact estimate. The fab subsequently returned to normal operations.
What 3nm Means: Density, Power, and Why Artificial Intelligence Drives It
A 3nm chip is not merely a faster version of a 6nm chip. The performance gap is structural. TSMC's N3 process delivers 70% logic density over 5nm, plus a 15% performance improvement at the same transistor count, and a 30% reduction in power consumption compared to its 5nm node — the previous generation widely used in high-performance AI chips.
For AI workloads — the inference and training pipelines that power large language models, image generators, and autonomous systems — transistor density and power efficiency are the primary engineering constraints. More transistors per square millimeter means more compute per die; lower power per transistor means larger dies can be built without exceeding thermal limits. The combination makes 3nm the node at which AI accelerators cross from constrained to capable at the scale AI infrastructure requires.
TSMC CEO C.C. Wei met Prime Minister Takaichi in Tokyo in February 2026 to signal the shift in direction, citing "strong demand driven by AI" as the driving rationale for moving the second Kumamoto fab from 6nm to 3nm. Japan's PM Office stated that "there is a huge significance to have the world's most advanced semiconductor factory in Japan from the perspective of economic security."
By installing 3nm capacity in Japan, TSMC can serve GPU and AI accelerator customers who require geographically diversified supply chains, while also positioning the facility to capture Japanese hyperscaler and defense-adjacent demand. JASM's ownership structure — TSMC holds 86.5% of JASM with Sony Semiconductor Solutions at 6%, Denso at 5.5%, and Toyota at approximately 2% — ensures that Japan's largest technology, automotive, and electronics companies have direct investment stakes in the outcome.
