BANGKOK, Oct. 19 (NNN-Yonhap) -- South Korea's economic growth could exceed projections by international organisations, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), barring unexpected external shocks, the finance minister has said, citing robust exports and facility investment data, Yonhap News Agency reported.
Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il made the assessment during a meeting with reporters in Bangkok on Friday. He visited Thailand to attend the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group last week, marking his first participation in a major international event since taking office last month.
His remarks came after the IMF projected South Korea's economy would grow 3.3 percent this year, raising its forecast by 0.7 percentage point from its July projection amid the global semiconductor supercycle.
"I believe exports and facility investment remained robust in the third quarter," the minister said.
"If that is the case, we think growth could exceed the 3.3 percent projected by the IMF," Lee said. "Barring new external events that significantly impact the economy, I think even the mid-3 percent range could be possible."
Lee later hinted that the mid-3 percent range would cover figures from 3.4 percent to 3.6 percent.
The finance minister said South Korea's economy grew 1.8 percent and 0.6 percent in the first and second quarters, respectively, noting annual growth could exceed expectations if the momentum continued into the third quarter, for which signs were already positive.
Lee added the country's potential growth rate could soon rebound.
"Given recent growth trends and the composition of growth, I believe our potential growth rate could reverse its downward trend and rebound," Lee said. "That turning point is approaching and may even be imminent."
The potential growth rate refers to the potential rate of increase in the GDP a country can sustain by fully utilising labor, capital and other resources without triggering inflation.
Lee said officials he met during the event, including representatives of credit rating agencies and multilateral development banks, offered positive assessments of South Korea's robust economic growth amid the country's strong chip exports.
"We exchanged views on the South Korean economy with officials from various countries," Lee said.
"Most agreed when I said growth might not be sustainable without addressing disparities and that I intended to focus on the issue," Lee said.
The finance minister said those he met noted how much progress South Korea makes in addressing disparities would depend on the government's efforts, but its attention to the issue itself could help sustain growth momentum.
When asked to identify a specific area of focus in addressing disparities, the finance minister said all sectors are closely linked, making the issue difficult to resolve.
"To tackle these challenges, we are seeking to implement social policies in three key areas, namely housing, jobs and financial services for vulnerable groups, which would likely cover most issues," Lee said.
The finance minister particularly stressed the need to address disparities in the job market, as they are linked to income gaps and disparities across regions and businesses.

After US September inflation data came in higher than expected, the market reassessed the Federal Reserve's rate path, sending US Treasury yields higher and putting pressure on tech stock valuations. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are large-cap semiconductor companies on the KOSPI, and their stock price fluctuations have a noticeable impact on the index.
Meanwhile, the market has turned its attention to the financing costs and return on capital expenditures for AI data center construction, with investors divided on whether demand for AI chips can sustain high-speed growth.
CXMT recently disclosed progress on its 4F² DRAM technology and plans to advance server DDR5 products. Its mass production timeline, yield rates, and customer certifications remain unclear. articles.full_text:
Authored On

Chipmakers face competition too fierce to carry regional development duties
Rapidus needs high-volume customers more than local supplier quotas
Korea’s Honam cluster tracks votes while power lines lag
In the late 1980s, Japanese manufacturers held nearly 50% of the global semiconductor market, while in recent years their share has hovered around 10%, according to data cited by the Brookings Institution. Japan lost most of its chip market share in a generation and now it wants back in at the cutting edge and at the same time is being asked to act as a regional policy tool. The Development Bank of Japan recorded in January 2026 that local businesses in Kyushu did not see the volume of work they expected from TSMC's plant in Kumamoto and the finding is now being used as an argument for Rapidus to tie up with the Hokkaido economy before it even released the first commercial chip. In South Korea, President Lee Jae-myung sided with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to announce an 800 trillion won plan in Gwangju and South Jeolla, a region with minimal semiconductor industrial infrastructure. There is one question both countries seem to be avoiding: who bears the costs when a factory is a quarter late in a market that expects no one.
The Semiconductor Industry Counts Every Delay in Market Share
TrendForce's second-quarter figures show just how little time chipmakers have to spare. TSMC collected 72.5% of the revenue of the ten largest foundries, with revenue close to $40.2 billion and a quarterly increase of 12.1%. Samsung remained second, but its share fell from 6.5% to 5.9% in three months because its revenue grew just 1.8% in a market that grew 11.5% overall. Just below is China's SMIC with 5.4% and a 20% increase in revenue in the quarter, despite operating without EUV lithography machines due to equipment export restrictions. The gap between the second- and third-place chipmakers is now half a percentage point and the third-place company is powered by the Chinese electronics chain, which bought upfront for PCs and laptops in the same quarter.
Memory chips tell much the same story, Korea looked untouchable here for years, but that lead is being tested. Counterpoint Research estimated that China's CXMT's DRAM revenue grew by over 700% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026 and that its share more than doubled to 8%, in a quarter where the total DRAM market reached a record $97 billion. Samsung holds the top spot with 38%, yet the rise of a fourth supplier backed by strong domestic demand and rapid capacity expansion makes every HBM line opened on time more valuable than ever and every late line more expensive. SK hynix surpassed Samsung in market value in June for the first time in over 25 years thanks to its lead in HBM, a lead built on investment decisions made earlier than its competitors.
The timing problem is even clearer in advanced logic chips. TSMC started mass production at the 2-nanometer node at Kaohsiung's Fab 22 in the fourth quarter of 2025, as confirmed by the company itself and is preparing the N2P and A16 versions for the second half of 2026. Rapidus is targeting the second half of fiscal year 2027 for the IIM-1 plant in Chitose, which, according to Tom's Hardware's analysis, places it about two years behind both TSMC and Samsung, in a hub where customers can already buy elsewhere with proven performance.
Rapidus Needs Customers Before It Needs Local Suppliers
The Japanese government has already committed to Rapidus 2,6 trillion yen in fees and investments by the end of the fiscal year ending in March 2027, according to Bloomberg calculations based on an announcement by the relevant ministry. On April 11, 2026, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry approved an additional support of 631,5 billion yen, bringing total state aid for research and development to 2,354 trillion yen, according to Reuters. On top of them came two capital injections from the state-owned IPA, 100 billion yen in February and 150 billion in June, as well as 167,6 billion from 32 private companies, including Canon, Fujitsu, NTT, SoftBank and Sony. These funds are used to pay lithography tools, clean spaces and engineer salaries, while demand for the company's chips is still the open issue. The CEO has named, as TrendForce conveyed by Hokkaido Shimbun, IBM and startup Tenstorrent as the most likely customers, Bloomberg reported that the April approval is intended for work on behalf of Fujitsu and during the analysis of Tom's Hardware no high-volume customers have yet been committed.
That is where the proposal to tie future aid to local suppliers comes in, including the certification of suppliers from Hokkaido and long-term local supply contracts, which may sound reasonable to regional officials but also shifts additional costs onto Rapidus, costs that don't really appear anywhere in the public budget. Certifying a chemical or spare parts supplier for a production line at 2 nanometers requires months of testing and a purity problem in a single material is enough to bring down the performance of an entire batch of tiles. Japan already has world-class suppliers, as according to the Brookings Institution it owns 88% of the coating and display device market through Tokyo Electron and Screen, 53% of silicon wafers through Shin-Etsu and Sumco and 50% of photoresist materials, so a term that favors the supplier's origin from a particular island over its quality takes options away from a company that has a single factory and no alternative location if the hub doesn't go ahead. The American design firms that Rapidus hopes to win will compare yields and delivery times with TSMC and none will ask how many of its suppliers are based in Hokkaido.
Some of this is already happening without the government stepping in anyway and in Kumamoto, TSMC had attracted additional investment from 44 companies by 2024, according to Taiwanese sources cited by the Brookings Institution, without being obliged by any procurement conditions. Suppliers follow the customer when they think there will be volume and will come in greater numbers if Rapidus shows returns that stand up to Taiwanese ones. If it fails, local businesses that have invested in machinery and personnel under a state-guaranteed contract will find themselves tied to a customer with no customers and the risk will have simply been transferred from Tokyo to the island's small and medium-sized companies.
Kumamoto Shows That Infrastructure Is the State’s Job
Kumamoto offers perhaps the best argument for the other side, as JASM, the subsidiary of TSMC with a minority stake in Sony, Denso and Toyota, started mass production at its first factory in Kikuyo in late 2024 and a few months later the start of construction of the second plant, scheduled for the first quarter of 2025, was postponed. TSMC CEO Shi Shi Wei publicly attributed the delay to the traffic jam caused by the first plant and the protests of residents, as recorded by TrendForce. The Development Bank of Japan, in its study of the Kyushu semiconductor industry, noted that along with rising land prices and investment in equipment, local businesses did not see the increase in jobs they expected. Those who ask companies to integrate into local economies read in this evidence that a factory without a local fabric ends up stumbling upon the very area that hosts it.
The roads around Kikuyo, water and housing for workers are public infrastructure and their inability to follow the investment is a planning failure of the state and prefecture, for which TSMC had neither the competence nor the tools. The cost was paid first by the company itself and its customers, who were waiting for the new capacity and were informed of the postponement. The Development Bank's study additionally identifies as a key obstacle the lack of semiconductor end-users in the region, i.e. a demand problem that no local procurement obligation solves and Taiwan's Economic Daily News had already written that few Japanese customers needed the advanced nodes originally planned for the second plant. JASM had already set a 60% local procurement target at its 2024 inauguration, according to the Brookings Institution and this goal did not change the basic market equation.
TSMC responded to low local demand by upgrading the hub instead, which makes sense really. On March 31, 2026, Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs approved the installation of the 3-nanometer process at Kumamoto's second plant, starting in 2028 and having a capacity of 15,000 12-inch tiles per month, in place of the original plan for nodes from 6 to 12 nanometers. Shi Shi Wei had explained to Premier Sanae Takaichi in February that the change responds to the explosive global demand for artificial intelligence and Nikkei has noted that most of TSMC's peak customers are American companies. What keeps the Kumamoto project viable, though, is global demand. Not demand from Kyushu alone.
For the Japanese Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and for the Hokkaido Prefecture, the practical lesson is to link public money to landmarks controlled by the public sector itself, i.e. kilometers of road, cubic meters of water, megawatts of grid connection and homes ready before the first shifts arrive and not to local procurement rates that a company with a factory and without a high-volume committed customer will have to fulfill. A public sector that has not delivered its own projects in Kumamoto on time can hardly ask Rapidus to undertake additional shipments in Chitose, especially when the country's own semiconductor industry has yet to prove that it can produce at 2 nanometers on commercial terms.

$35 Million Investment Will Expand Axcelis' Manufacturing Capacity and Enable the Company to Better Serve Customers
BEVERLY, Mass., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Axcelis Technologies, Inc. (Nasdaq: ACLS), a leading supplier of enabling ion implantation solutions for the semiconductor industry, today announced that it will officially break ground on its new ion implantation equipment manufacturing facility in Pyeongtaek, Gyeonggi Province, Korea. This $35 million investment reflects Axcelis' continued commitment to strengthening its high-volume manufacturing infrastructure and expanding its capacity to serve customers around the world.
The Pyeongtaek site will expand Axcelis' current manufacturing operations in Korea, the Axcelis Asia Operations Center. The new facility will encompass approximately 200,000 square feet of total gross floor area. The manufacturing center's design will provide a lean production environment that integrates learnings from the Company's nearly 50 years of semiconductor capital equipment experience. The Pyeongtaek facility will include warehousing, cleanrooms, and a training center to enable fast and flexible responses to customers' needs. Production at the new manufacturing facility is scheduled to commence in the second half of 2028.
President and CEO Russell Low commented, "We are proud to celebrate this pivotal moment for Axcelis and the next chapter of our growth in Korea. As the global economy enters the AI era, leadership in advanced semiconductors will be a cornerstone of technological progress and economic growth. This new facility will expand our ability to serve customers while building on the ingenuity of our people, whose work helps enable breakthrough technologies and a more sustainable, prosperous future for all."
Governor of Gyeonggi Province Choo Mi Ae stated, "I would like to extend my sincere congratulations on the groundbreaking of Axcelis Korea's Pyeongtaek facility. Axcelis' investment in advanced semiconductor process equipment represents a significant milestone in strengthening the position of Gyeonggi Province and Pyeongtaek City as global hubs for the semiconductor industry. In particular, we expect this project to contribute greatly not only to the creation of high-quality jobs and the revitalization of the local economy, but also to enhance the competitiveness of the world's leading semiconductor ecosystem. Gyeonggi Province will continue to foster a business-friendly environment and provide efficient administrative support to help Axcelis achieve sustainable growth and long-term success in Korea. Once again, congratulations on this groundbreaking ceremony. I wish Axcelis every success in its business expansion and continued prosperity in the years ahead."

According to the Korea Exchange on the 20th, individual investors net purchased the KOSPI worth 100.7123 trillion won until this day. At the end of last year, more than 10% of the time deposit balance (about 939 trillion won based on the five major banks) flowed into the KOSPI for the first time in a year. This is well above the largest net purchase ever recorded in 2021, 65.9021 trillion won, thanks to the Donghak Ant Movement.
Most of the domestic stock market investment by individual investors this year went to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Until the 19th of this year, individual net purchases by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix amounted to 48.1731 trillion won and 42.8396 trillion won, respectively. The stock prices of the two stocks are still in the 70-80% range compared to the beginning of the year. However, compared to the high point, it fell 41.7% and 58.1%, respectively.
In particular, it is fatal that buying has been concentrated near the high point. The reality is different despite the high stock price increase compared to the beginning of the year. Many individual investors are trapped in the principal loss section. According to the monthly figures, a large inflow of funds took place between May and June, just before entering the plunge in July. For two months, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix absorbed more than 32 trillion won and 38 trillion won in personal funds, respectively.
Hyundai Motor (12.3275 trillion won), the third-largest net buyer this year, is also recording a 58.7% drop from its peak. Power device and semiconductor substrate industries such as LS Electric (-48.3%) and LG Innotek (-72.4%) entered the adjustment market in May after showing a steep rise in expectations of expanding investment in AI data centers. Similarly, LG Electronics, which had a steep rally on expectations for robotics and AI data center chiller businesses, also fell 58.4 percent from its peak. Since then, semiconductors have collapsed without hesitation as AI profitability skepticism in July and a sharp decline due to AI credit risk amid high interest rates this month.
KOSDAQ is in a situation where losses are more serious. All of the top 10 net purchases on the KOSDAQ fell more than 50% from their high points. In particular, there was a sharp rise due to the concentration of individual buying on newly listed stocks, but the pattern of plunging to or below the public offering price was repeated.
RZnomics, which was listed at the end of last year and ranked first in the number of individual net purchases on KOSDAQ this year, saw its stock price fall 80.2% from its peak. Compared to the beginning of the year, it has also fallen by 70.8%. Even before going public, RZnomics signed a large-scale technology transfer contract with Eli Lilly and had a steep rally in the first half of the year. However, the stock price plunged in late March as semiconductor concentration accelerated along with the problem of unfaithful disclosure in the same industry. Since then, global pharmaceutical company Biogen's phase 2 RNA Alzheimer's drug has only been half successful, and the stock price has been on a steeper decline.
Top-ranked bio stocks such as ABL Bio (-77.7%) and Kolon TissueGene (-80.6%) also plunged 70-80% from the beginning of the year. Stocks that showed steep rallies this year, such as Korea Telecom (498.0%) and Woori Technology (172.3%), fell 56.2% and 66.2%, respectively, compared to their high points. Cosmorobotics, which went public in May, is 7.0% lower than the offering price, but its drop from its high point was 90.1%, the largest among the top 10 stocks.
Despite such a "continuous investment streak," individual investors are continuing to buy low prices mainly in semiconductors and leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) despite the plunge this month. Until the 20th of this month, the KOSPI net purchased 7.1318 trillion won. Investors seeking a technological rebound along with excessive perception of the fall continue to flow in.
Yang Hyun-kyung, a researcher at iM Securities, said, "The U.S. stock market closed mixed last night due to the influx of backlash buying into semiconductor and AI-related stocks, which plunged last week," adding, "The burden of AI credit continues, but low-priced buying is expected to continue mainly in semiconductors."

articles.title: [Interview] Korea's alliance with US is evolving, not breaking down, says unification minister - 한겨레
articles.summary: [Interview] Korea's alliance with US is evolving, not breaking down, says unification minister  한겨레
articles.full_text:
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young speaks to the Hankyoreh for an exclusive interview at the ministry's Inter-Korean Relations Management Bureau in Seoul on Oct. 14, 2026. (Jung Yong-il/Hankyoreh)
          Unification Minister Chung Dong-young called on politicians to move past the partisan red-versus-blue divide amid recent friction between South Korean and US intelligence authorities, in an exclusive interview with the Hankyoreh on Wednesday at his ministry’s Inter-Korean Relations Management Bureau in Seoul.
Chung said friction could arise as the Korea-US alliance moves away from the one-sided relationship of the past 73 years toward one built on mutual benefit, and that portraying the current strain as a breakdown of the alliance was “overkill.”
He noted that Trump views the alliance in “transactional” terms, which he said was not necessarily a bad thing. But he questioned whether Washington was using the intelligence-sharing dispute as leverage in negotiations aimed at short-term gains, such as securing Korean investment in the US.
On the prospects of a summit between North Korea and the US, discussed in connection with next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, the minister said the Ministry of Unification considers such a meeting “within reach.”
Chung said Seoul should use a North Korea-US summit as a springboard toward four-party talks among the two Koreas, the US and China, and stressed that an inter-Korean summit must take place during President Lee Jae Myung’s term.
Turning to strained Seoul-Pyongyang relations, the minister said he had expected to achieve at least a small breakthrough within about a year of taking office, but that the two sides remain at a stalemate. He pointed to a recent statement by Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, which said the South must show respect, consideration and sincerity if it wants relations to thaw. In response, Chung said trust can grow only if the North stops slandering Lee and treats the South with mutual respect and consideration in turn.
Hankyoreh: Conservative opposition parties are calling for you and National Intelligence Service (NIS) Director Lee Jong-seok to be dismissed following concerns over unusually strained intelligence cooperation between Korea and the US. 
Chung: The forces that benefit from the divided peninsula and have entrenched interests are attempting to wield their authority arbitrarily. The NIS announced there were no issues with a reciprocal sharing of intelligence that is mutually beneficial. The Defense Ministry has also announced that there are no restrictions on intelligence sharing that affect our military readiness. Trying to frame the situation in a way that insinuates that the alliance has become broken beyond repair is overkill. Trump treats the alliance as a transactional relationship. While that is not necessarily a bad thing, I cannot help but wonder if the US is using this issue as a bargaining chip in various negotiations aimed at securing short-term benefits, such as Korea’s investment in the US.
Hankyoreh: Would it be reasonable to say that the US is putting pressure on Korea to confirm its investment in various projects such as the Alaska LNG pipeline before the November midterms?
Chung: One could say that.
Hankyoreh: The White House recently announced that it expected Korea to “uphold the standards of [the] decades-long alliance, in particular concerning matters of intelligence and counterintelligence.” What does that imply?
Chung: For the past 73 years, the Korea-US alliance has been a one-sided, one-way alliance. We are now in the process of transitioning to a mutually beneficial alliance. That is the future we must pursue for a more stable alliance. Tensions will likely arise during that process. We must not allow ourselves to become dependent on the alliance. Our alliances must put our national interest and autonomy at the forefront.
Hankyoreh: North Korea’s Kim Yo-jong has slammed the mine explosion in the DMZ as a “farce.” Some are criticizing you for being too deferential.
Chung: During the seven years since the 2019 inter-Korean summit, not so much as a single ant has been able to cross the border, and we have been unable to make even the tiniest of breakthroughs. How are we supposed to build trust if we constantly fuss over each other’s every move? North Korea may seem to be taking a high-handed approach, but it needs to get along with its closest neighbor. After defining inter-Korean relations as being between two hostile states, the North has opted to ignore the opinion of those in the South. In a recent statement, Kim Yo-jong claimed that if we wanted to see inter-Korean relations thaw, the South must show respect, consideration and sincerity. To that, I say this: trust will flourish only when the North ceases its slanderous remarks against our president and also treats us with mutual respect and consideration. At present, the situation may seem frustrating, but we must press on and do what we can, holding on to the hope that things will change. I disagree with those who disparage this attitude as overly deferential.
Hankyoreh: Some are calling for the resumption of cyber sanctions and loudspeaker broadcasts against North Korea.
Chung: During the Yoon Suk-yeol administration, Korea implemented unilateral sanctions against the North on 24 occasions — basically once every month. In terms of efficacy, it yielded no significant results. The Lee Jae Myung administration is pursuing a policy of peaceful coexistence. How could we pursue peaceful coexistence while also implementing unilateral sanctions? As for loudspeaker broadcasts, even local government leaders from the People Power Party in border regions issued a statement calling for the cessation of such broadcasts, saying that we should not endanger residents in the border. We must not disrupt the peace of people’s daily lives.
Hankyoreh: Did you butt heads over this issue with Foreign Affairs Minister Cho Hyun during the National Security Council?
Chung: The confidentiality of the National Security Council has never been breached, not by any administration. These kinds of leaks are extremely regrettable.
              
              Unification Minister Chung Dong-young speaks to the Hankyoreh for an exclusive interview at the ministry's Inter-Korean Relations Management Bureau in Seoul on Oct. 14, 2026. (Jung Yong-il/Hankyoreh)
          
Hankyoreh: Following the mine explosion incident, it has been suggested that the two Koreas and the UN Command hold talks to define the Military Demarcation Line (MDL).
Chung: Isn’t that the most sensible response? The UN Command and the two Koreas should work together to demarcate the MDL. If North Korea refuses to cooperate with the South, then it should at least sit down at the table with the UN Command. If North Korea and the US successfully engage in talks this November, the issue of demarcating the MDL could become an agenda.
Hankyoreh: What are the odds of a North Korea-US summit?
Chung: The NIS believes it’s 50-50. The Unification Ministry believes that, based on various developments, a summit is within reach. However, the obstacle here is the North Korean Foreign Ministry’s passivity, given the failure to secure a deal during the previous Hanoi 2019 summit. 
During the 9th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea in February, Kim Jong-un stated that only a “cool-headed calculation and strict response for our national interests” remains in its relations with the South. In this context, national interest will likely refer to the right of survival and the right of development, such as the suspension of South Korea-US joint military exercises and the lifting of sanctions. Following the disastrous Hanoi 2019 summit, Kim declared that he would not be so fixated on the lifting of sanctions. 
In an interview with The New York Times in September, President Lee made clear his belief that there is “significant value in a trade-off between sanctions — which are not particularly effective anyway — and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology.”
As such, the president has opened the conversation on sanctions. A North Korea-US summit would be the first step in seeing this through.
Hankyoreh: What role should Seoul adopt in the future?
Chung: We must use the North Korea-US summit as a springboard to move toward four-party talks involving South Korea, North Korea, the US and China. Even if North Korea and the US successfully engage in talks, that will not immediately solve every single problem. There are various agenda items, including the normalization of North Korea-US relations, the establishment of a peace treaty, arms control, the goal of denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula and economic cooperation. Naturally, South Korea, North Korea, the US and China are the parties that should address these issues comprehensively. 
When Kim stated how the North was willing to “resume the Kaesong Industrial Park and Mt. Kumgang tourism without any precondition and in return for nothing,” during his 2019 New Year’s address, we should have taken control [instead of walking on eggshells around the US]. Our hesitation was the biggest strategic blunder.
There are some within the government who believe that we should stay still, wait and refrain from making any moves. I do not agree with such views. This will only lead us to failure. We must come up with creative alternatives and be more proactive.
Hankyoreh: Trump has previously hinted at acknowledging North Korea as a nuclear power, but, for South Korea, isn’t it something that we can’t acknowledge?
Chung: Right. The only nuclear-weapon states that exist are the US, China, the UK, France and Russia. We are parties to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Kim Jong-un also wants North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state to be respected,
